images.title: Every prime is shared out
images.purpose: Show that the primes of 12 and 18 split between the HCF (smaller count) and the LCM (larger count), so together they match the product.
images.composition: Two rows of prime tiles on the left, two boxes of tiles on the right joined by one grey arrow, and one equation line along the bottom, with white space between.
exact_structure: Left: row 12 = followed by exactly 3 tiles 2, 2, 3; row 18 = followed by exactly 3 tiles 2, 3, 3. Every 2 tile is teal #0072B2 and every 3 tile is amber #E69F00.
One grey #6B7280 arrow from the two rows to the right side.
Right top: a reddish purple #CC79A7 outlined box labelled HCF = 6 holding exactly 2 tiles: 2, 3.
Right bottom: a green #009E73 outlined box labelled LCM = 36 holding exactly 4 tiles: 2, 2, 3, 3.
On both sides every 2 tile is teal #0072B2 and every 3 tile is amber #E69F00, so the left has 3 teal and 3 amber tiles, and the right also has 3 teal and 3 amber tiles.
rejection: tile counts other than 3 and 3 on the left rows, 2 in the HCF box and 4 in the LCM box
the left and right sides not each having exactly 3 teal 2 tiles and 3 amber 3 tiles
an HCF other than 6, an LCM other than 36, or a product other than 216
the numbers 4, 6 and 10 shown as a three number example
images.takeaway: For each prime the HCF takes the smaller count and the LCM the larger, so together they use exactly the primes of the product.
images.description: 12 and 18 as prime tiles, shared out into an HCF box with 2, 3 and an LCM box with 2, 2, 3, 3, and 6 × 36 = 216 = 12 × 18.
images.context: Shown beside the concept text and video on why the rule works.
images.teaching_notes: Count the teal and amber tiles on each side; they match, which is why HCF × LCM equals the product.

image_decisions.why: Matching tile counts on both sides is the clearest picture of why the rule holds for two numbers.
